findings.title: AI threats in the wild: The current state of prompt injections on the web
findings.summary: Posted by Thomas Brunner, Yu-Han Liu, Moni Pande At Google, our Threat Intelligence teams are dedicated to staying ahead of real-world adversarial activity, proactively monitoring emerging threats before they can impact users. Right now, Indirect Prompt Injection (IPI) is a top priority for the security community, anticipating it as a primary attack vector for adversaries to target and compromise AI agents. But while the danger of IPI is widely discussed, are threat actors actually exploiting this vector today – and if so, how? To answer these questions and to uncover real-world abuse, we initiated a broad sweep of the public web to monitor for known indirect prompt injection patterns. This is what we found. The threat of indirect prompt injection Unlike a direct injection where a user "jailbreaks" a chatbot, IPI occurs when an AI system processes content—like a website, email, or document—that contains malicious instructions. When the AI reads this poisoned content, it may silently follow the attacker's commands instead of the user's original intent. This is not a new area of concern for us and Google has been working tirelessly to combat these threats. Our efforts involve cross-functional collaboration between researchers at Google DeepMind (GDM) and defenders like the Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG). We have previously detailed our work in this area and researchers have further highlighted the evolving nature of these vulnerabilities. Despite this collective focus, a fundamental question remains: to what degree are real-world malicious actors currently operationalizing these attacks? Proactive monitoring at Google The landscape of IPI on the web There are many channels through which attackers might try to send prompt injections. However, one location is particularly easy to observe - the public web. Here, threat actors may simply seed prompt injections on websites in hope of corrupting AI systems that browse them. findings.title: Google Workspace’s continuous approach to mitigating indirect prompt injections
findings.summary: Posted by Adam Gavish, Google GenAI Security Team Indirect prompt injection (IPI) is an evolving threat vector targeting users of complex AI applications with multiple data sources, such as Workspace with Gemini. This technique enables the attacker to influence the behavior of an LLM by injecting malicious instructions into the data or tools used by the LLM as it completes the user’s query. This may even be possible without any input directly from the user. IPI is not the kind of technical problem you “solve” and move on. Sophisticated LLMs with increasing use of agentic automation combined with a wide range of content create an ultra-dynamic and evolving playground for adversarial attacks. That’s why Google takes a sophisticated and comprehensive approach to these attacks. We’re continuously improving LLM resistance to IPI attacks and launching AI application capabilities with ever-improving defenses. Staying ahead of the latest indirect prompt injection attacks is critical to our mission of securing Workspace with Gemini. In our previous blog “ Mitigating prompt injection attacks with a layered defense strategy ”, we reviewed the layered architecture of our IPI defenses. In this blog, we’ll share more detail on the continuous approach we take to improve these defenses and to solve for new attacks. New attack discovery By proactively discovering and cataloging new attack vectors through internal and external programs, we can identify vulnerabilities and deploy robust defenses ahead of adversarial activity. Human Red-Teaming Human Red-Teaming uses adversarial simulations to uncover security and safety vulnerabilities. Specialized teams execute attacks based on realistic user profiles to exploit weaknesses, coordinating with product teams to resolve identified issues. findings.title: Architecting Security for Agentic Capabilities in Chrome
findings.summary: Posted by Nathan Parker, Chrome security team Chrome has been advancing the web’s security for well over 15 years, and we’re committed to meeting new challenges and opportunities with AI. Billions of people trust Chrome to keep them safe by default, and this is a responsibility we take seriously. Following the recent launch of Gemini in Chrome and the preview of agentic capabilities , we want to share our approach and some new innovations to improve the safety of agentic browsing. The primary new threat facing all agentic browsers is indirect prompt injection . It can appear in malicious sites, third-party content in iframes, or from user-generated content like user reviews, and can cause the agent to take unwanted actions such as initiating financial transactions or exfiltrating sensitive data. Given this open challenge, we are investing in a layered defense that includes both deterministic and probabilistic defenses to make it difficult and costly for attackers to cause harm. Designing safe agentic browsing for Chrome has involved deep collaboration of security experts across Google. We built on Gemini's existing protections and agent security principles and have implemented several new layers for Chrome. We’re introducing a user alignment critic where the agent’s actions are vetted by a separate model that is isolated from untrusted content. We’re also extending Chrome’s origin-isolation capabilities to constrain what origins the agent can interact with, to just those that are relevant to the task. Our layered defense also includes user confirmations for critical steps, real-time detection of threats , and red-teaming and response . We’ll step through these layers below. findings.title: Rust in Android: move fast and fix things
findings.summary: Posted by Jeff Vander Stoep, Android Last year, we wrote about why a memory safety strategy that focuses on vulnerability prevention in new code quickly yields durable and compounding gains. This year we look at how this approach isn’t just fixing things, but helping us move faster . The 2025 data continues to validate the approach, with memory safety vulnerabilities falling below 20% of total vulnerabilities for the first time. Updated data for 2025. This data covers first-party and third-party (open source) code changes to the Android platform across C, C++, Java, Kotlin, and Rust. This post is published a couple of months before the end of 2025, but Android’s industry-standard 90-day patch window means that these results are very likely close to final. We can and will accelerate patching when necessary. We adopted Rust for its security and are seeing a 1000x reduction in memory safety vulnerability density compared to Android’s C and C++ code . But the biggest surprise was Rust's impact on software delivery. With Rust changes having a 4x lower rollback rate and spending 25% less time in code review , the safer path is now also the faster one. In this post, we dig into the data behind this shift and also cover: How we’re expanding our reach: We're pushing to make secure code the default across our entire software stack. We have updates on Rust adoption in first-party apps, the Linux kernel, and firmware. It’s also a good chance to answer the question “if Rust can have memory safety issues, why bother at all?” Building Better Software, Faster Developing an operating system requires the low-level control and predictability of systems programming languages like C, C++, and Rust. findings.title: Mitigating prompt injection attacks with a layered defense strategy
findings.summary: Posted by Adam Gavish, Google GenAI Security Team With the rapid adoption of generative AI, a new wave of threats is emerging across the industry with the aim of manipulating the AI systems themselves. One such emerging attack vector is indirect prompt injections. Unlike direct prompt injections, where an attacker directly inputs malicious commands into a prompt, indirect prompt injections involve hidden malicious instructions within external data sources. These may include emails, documents, or calendar invites that instruct AI to exfiltrate user data or execute other rogue actions. As more governments, businesses, and individuals adopt generative AI to get more done, this subtle yet potentially potent attack becomes increasingly pertinent across the industry, demanding immediate attention and robust security measures. At Google, our teams have a longstanding precedent of investing in a defense-in-depth strategy, including robust evaluation, threat analysis, AI security best practices , AI red-teaming , adversarial training, and model hardening for generative AI tools. This approach enables safer adoption of Gemini in Google Workspace and the Gemini app (we refer to both in this blog as “Gemini” for simplicity). Below we describe our prompt injection mitigation product strategy based on extensive research, development, and deployment of improved security mitigations. A layered security approach Google has taken a layered security approach introducing security measures designed for each stage of the prompt lifecycle. From Gemini 2.5 model hardening, to purpose-built machine learning (ML) models detecting malicious instructions, to system-level safeguards, we are meaningfully elevating the difficulty, expense, and complexity faced by an attacker. This approach compels adversaries to resort to methods that are either more easily identified or demand greater resources. findings.summary: Russian State-Supported Cyber Actors Conduct Phishing Campaign Targeting Users of Zimbra Collaboration Suite Executive summary A group of Russian state-supported cyber actors has been targeting and compromising various Western government and commercial organizations using the Zimbra Collaboration Suite (ZCS) software since at least July 2025. The Russian state-supported advanced persistent threat (APT) group’s activity is tracked in the cybersecurity community under several names (see Cybersecurity industry tracking ), primarily as “LAUNDRY BEAR,” a name initially coined by the Netherlands General Intelligence and Security Service (AIVD) and Defence Intelligence and Security Service (MIVD) [ 1 ]. LAUNDRY BEAR’s targeting is almost certainly to gather sensitive information for the Russian Federation, with these actors primarily focusing on the covert acquisition of email data. Previous campaigns indicated LAUNDRY BEAR relied on unsophisticated initial access techniques—including password spraying, phishing, and pass-the-cookie—allowing the group to successfully run high-volume operations. The latest campaign targeting ZCS uses a novel exploit that was a zero-day vulnerability when first exploited and continues to be successfully exploited. The vulnerability, Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVE) CVE-2025-66376 , was patched in November 2025. This demonstrates LAUNDRY BEAR’s intent and ability to deploy increasingly sophisticated technical capabilities. Unlike traditional phishing campaigns that persuade a user into taking an action, such as clicking a link or opening a file, LAUNDRY BEAR’s latest campaign leverages a view-based exploit that only requires a user to view a malicious email within a vulnerable version of the webmail service. findings.title: Active Storage: Possible arbitrary file write and read in image analysis
findings.summary:
### Impact
A Rails application that processes attachments with ImageMagick may allow an unauthenticated attacker to write arbitrary files on the server and, when attachments are stored with the Disk service, to read arbitrary files readable by the application process. Those files typically include `secret_key_base` and credentials for external systems, which may in turn allow escalation to remote code execution or lateral movement to those systems.

### Details
ImageMagick selects a coder from the content of the file it is given, and some coders act on files named inside the image rather than on the image itself. Active Storage constrained none of ImageMagick's coders, and the ImageMagick analyzer runs when a file is attached, so an attacker who can upload a crafted file may be able to invoke one. Attaching the upload is sufficient; no variant, preview, or `analyze` call is required. One specific attack chain has been reported to us, but we do not assume it is the only one that exists.

The fixed versions ship an ImageMagick security policy and prepend its directory to `MAGICK_CONFIGURE_PATH` through `MiniMagick.cli_env`, so every ImageMagick process that MiniMagick spawns applies it. The policy denies the `MSL` scripting coder, the coders that read or delete files other than the image, fetch remote or local references, or display to a screen, every coder backed by Ghostscript together with the `gs` delegate, and `@filename` indirection. ImageMagick applies every `policy.xml` on its search path, so the shipped policy adds to the host's policy rather than replacing it. The policy applies to every ImageMagick command that MiniMagick runs, not only those of Active Storage. See the `activestorage` CHANGELOG and "ImageMagick Security Policy" in the Active Storage guide.

### Affected applications
An application is affected if it meets all of these requirements:
- Uses ImageMagick for Active Storage image processing. This is `config.active_storage.variant_processor = :min

findings.title: Action Pack: Possible sensitive session information leak in Active Storage proxy mode
findings.summary:
### Impact
When `ActionDispatch::Cookies` reads a signed or encrypted cookie that was written under a rotated secret (`config.action_dispatch.cookies_rotations`) or in the format that a `:hybrid` cookie serializer migrates from, it writes the cookie back to the response in the current format, and that write ignores `request.session_options[:skip]`. `ActiveStorage::DisableSession` relies on that option to keep the session cookie off the public, immutable responses of the Active Storage proxy controllers, but those controllers still load the session, so a request carrying an old-format session cookie could receive the rewritten session cookie in `Set-Cookie` on a cacheable response. A shared cache that stores such a response together with its `Set-Cookie` header could then serve one user's session to later requesters of the same URL, or serve an attacker's session to other users.

Applications are affected when they serve Active Storage files through the proxy controllers, have a cookie rotation or a `:hybrid` serializer migration configured, and run behind a cache that stores `Set-Cookie` on public responses. This is a path around the fix for [CVE-2024-26144](https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-8h22-8cf7-hq6g).

### Details
In the fixed releases, a response that skips the session leaves an old-format signed or encrypted cookie unchanged, and the next request that does not skip the session upgrades it. An application that skips the session on every request no longer upgrades its signed or encrypted cookies. Cookies that the application sets explicitly are still written. See the Action Pack CHANGELOG.

### Workarounds
Configure caching proxies not to store responses that carry a `Set-Cookie` header, or complete the cookie rotation or serializer migration and remove it from the configuration.

### Releases
The fixed releases are available at the normal locations.

Patches for those who cannot upgrade at once:
- 8.1: https://github.com/rails/rails/commit/849a6c30eacbb6ca4

findings.title: Pillow: Memory DoS in TIFF and EXIF IFD parsing via overlapping tag data
findings.summary:
```
============================================================================
ANT-2026-D7STJUWL  [medium]  CWE-770  dos
Memory DoS in TIFF and EXIF IFD parsing via overlapping tag data
Location: src/PIL/TiffImagePlugin.py:927  in ImageFileDirectory_v2.load()
Commit:   a707c6b21c313880d0771e54965d142dd42358b6
============================================================================
```

A small, crafted image file can make Pillow use thousands of times its own size in memory while the file is only being opened, which lets anyone who can submit an image crash or stall the process handling it. A 144 KB TIFF makes `Image.open()` return normally while holding 1.6 GiB of memory. The largest such standard TIFF, about 786 KB, asks for roughly 48 GiB, which in practice gets the worker killed by the operating system. The file declares a 1×1 image, so the decompression-bomb check never triggers and no warning is raised. There is no memory corruption; the impact is denial of service.

The bug is in `ImageFileDirectory_v2.load()` in `src/PIL/TiffImagePlugin.py` (around line 927). For every directory entry whose value is stored elsewhere in the file, it reads that value into a new `bytes` object with `ImageFile._safe_read(fp, count * unit_size)` and keeps it in `_tagdata`. `_safe_read()` only checks that the bytes exist. Nothing limits the total read across entries, and nothing stops every entry from pointing at the same bytes. An attacker can therefore give each of N distinct private tags an offset and count that covers the whole file, at a cost of 12 bytes per entry. Memory grows as N × file size, which is quadratic in the file size, and BigTIFF removes the 65,535-entry ceiling.

The same loop parses EXIF data, so the problem reaches beyond TIFF:

* A 66 KB JPEG APP1 segment costs about 340 MiB inside `Image.open()` itself, via `_read_dpi_from_exif()`.
* A 96 KB PNG `eXIf` chunk costs 754 MiB on `getexif()` or `ImageOps.exif_transpose()`.

findings.title: Pillow: Heap buffer overflow saving TIFF with libtiff when tags override image size
findings.summary:
```
============================================================================
ANT-2026-CS7N494P  [high]  CWE-787  memory-safety
Heap buffer overflow saving TIFF with libtiff when tags override image size
Location: src/libImaging/TiffDecode.c:1035  in ImagingLibTiffEncode()
Commit:   a707c6b21c313880d0771e54965d142dd42358b6
============================================================================
```

When Pillow saves an image as a compressed TIFF, size information taken from the image's metadata can make the encoder read past the end of a heap buffer. Someone who uploads an image can use this to get the server process's memory, including pointers, copied into the saved file, or to crash the process. When the metadata also enables TIFF "Predictor=2" compression, the encoder writes past the buffer instead, corrupting the heap and aborting the process. This affects applications that write TIFF through libtiff (any `compression=` other than raw) and either carry the source metadata across with `exif=im.getexif()` / `tiffinfo=`, or simply re-save a crafted palette TIFF with `Image.open(f).save(out, "TIFF")`, which inherits its compression and predictor from the upload.

In `TiffImagePlugin._save`'s libtiff branch, only `BitsPerSample` is pinned to the real image when the tag list for the encoder is built (`src/PIL/TiffImagePlugin.py:1955`). `ImageWidth`, `ImageLength` and `PlanarConfiguration` are set from `im.size` but are then overwritten by the `exif=`/`tiffinfo=` merge loop at `:1768-1772`. `SamplesPerPixel` is never set for single-band modes, so a value from the caller's tags or from the source TIFF's own IFD reaches `TIFFSetField`. `ImagingLibTiffEncode` then passes a row buffer sized from the actual image (`src/encode.c:291`) to `TIFFWriteScanline` (`src/libImaging/TiffDecode.c:1035`) with no check against `TIFFScanlineSize()`, and libtiff consumes a full scanline of the tag-described width from it.

findings.title: Hono: `mount()` and `app.mount()` can forward a path that bypasses middleware scoped inside the mount prefix
findings.summary:
### Summary

`mount()` and `app.mount()` remove the mount prefix from the request path and forward the rest to the mounted application. Two mistakes in that step let a crafted request reach a route of the mounted application that the outer application protects with path-scoped middleware, such as an authentication check on `/app/admin/*`. The outer application routes on the original path, so the middleware does not run.

### Details

1. **Dynamic prefix** (all affected versions): for a mount such as `/api/:tenant/*`, the prefix was removed by the length of the route pattern, not of the matched prefix. A request with a longer or shorter first segment is cut in the middle, so `/api/a/xxxxx/admin/secret` reaches the mounted application as `/admin/secret`.
2. **Re-normalization** (since 4.12.21): the forwarded path was built from the decoded request path and assigned to `url.pathname`, which turns a decoded backslash into `/` and collapses `..`. `/app/public%5C..%5Cadmin/secret` reaches the mounted application as `/admin/secret`.

The fix removes the prefix segment by segment from the raw pathname, using the matched parameter values for its length. Route patterns that cannot be handled safely now throw: duplicate parameter names and a wildcard inside the last segment such as `/assets*`. A trailing slash in an `app.mount()` prefix no longer removes an extra segment.

### Impact

An unauthenticated client can reach a route of a mounted application that the outer application protects with path-scoped middleware.

This affects applications that use `mount()` or `app.mount()` and rely on middleware registered on a sub-path inside the mount prefix for authentication or authorization.

### Workarounds

Register the authentication middleware inside the mounted application.

findings.title: Addressable URI normalization resolves some dotted path segments to the wrong path
findings.summary:
### Summary

`Addressable::URI.normalize_path` resolves some paths containing `..` segments to a different path than RFC 3986 does. When a path climbs above the root before any other `..` is resolved, the segments that later `..` segments should remove are instead kept: `/../../public/x/../../secret` normalizes to `/public/x/secret` instead of `/secret`. `URI#normalize`, `URI#join`, `URI#==` and `URI#===` all use this normalization. An application that checks a normalized Addressable path against an allowlist, but sends the original URI to something that resolves it according to RFC 3986, can be made to allow a request for a path outside the allowlist.

### Details

`normalize_path` in 2.9.0 (`lib/addressable/uri.rb`) removes dot segments by repeating a set of rewrites until nothing changes. On each pass it finds the first `/segment/../` pair with `RULE_2B_2C`, then replaces every textual copy of that pair in the path with `/`:

```ruby
pair = normalized_path.match(RULE_2B_2C)
...
regexp = "/#{Regexp.escape(parent.to_s)}/\\.\\./|"
regexp += "(/#{Regexp.escape(current.to_s)}/\\.\\.$)"
...
mod ||= normalized_path.gsub!(Regexp.new(regexp), SLASH)
```

When the first pair found is `/../../`, where the "segment" is itself `..`, every `/../../` in the path is replaced with `/`. That includes copies later in the path, where each `..` should have removed the segment before it. For `/../../public/x/../../secret`:

- RFC 3986 §5.2.4 drops the two leading `..` segments, which can't go above the root, then removes `x` and `public`, giving `/secret`.
- 2.9.0 replaces both copies of `/../../` with `/` in one step, giving `/public/x/secret`.

Paths where an ordinary `/segment/../` pair comes first, such as `/a/../../b/c/../../d`, are resolved correctly.

This was introduced in 2.2.5. Versions 2.0.0 through 2.2.4 and earlier versions resolve these paths correctly. It is fixed in 2.9.1, which replaces the rewrite loop with a single pass that correctly follows RFC 3986 §5.2.4.

findings.title: @hono/node-server: Backslash in the request path is parsed as a path separator, bypassing path-based access control at a reverse proxy
findings.summary:
### Summary

`@hono/node-server` passes the raw request-target to the WHATWG URL parser, which treats a backslash in the path as `/` and then resolves `..` segments. A request for `/admin\secret` or `/public\..\admin/secret` reaches the application as `/admin/secret`. A reverse proxy that follows RFC 3986 forwards the backslash unchanged and applies its path-based rules to the original path, so the request reaches a route the proxy is meant to block.

### Details

A raw backslash is not allowed in a request-target (RFC 3986, RFC 9112 Section 3.2.1), and RFC 9112 Section 3.2 says a recipient should reject such a request rather than correct it. Proxies such as nginx on Linux, HAProxy and Envoy keep the backslash as an ordinary character, so they and the application see different paths.

The fix responds with `400 Bad Request` to a request whose path contains a raw backslash, for HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2, absolute-form request-targets and WebSocket upgrades. A percent-encoded backslash and a backslash in the query string are still accepted.

### Impact

An unauthenticated client can reach a route that a reverse proxy, load balancer or WAF in front of the application blocks by path.

This affects applications served by `@hono/node-server` behind a front component that makes path-based decisions and forwards a backslash unchanged. Access control inside the Hono application, such as middleware on `/admin/*`, runs on the rewritten path and is not affected.

findings.title: Loofah: SVG `<textPath>` and `<mpath>` bypass local-reference restriction
findings.summary:
## Summary

Loofah restricts `href` and `xlink:href` on certain SVG elements to same-document references. Two elements escaped the restriction:

- `<textPath>`: `SVG_ALLOW_LOCAL_HREF` listed it in lowercase as `textpath`, but the HTML5 parser names the element `textPath` inside `<svg>`, so the check never matched on the HTML5 path.
- `<mpath>`: absent from `SVG_ALLOW_LOCAL_HREF`, so its references were never restricted on either path.

`rails-html-sanitizer` reuses this safelist in its `PermitScrubber`, so it is affected too.

## Impact

An external `href` or `xlink:href` on `<textPath>` or `<mpath>` survives sanitization. Firefox fetches the URL when rendering the content, which leaks the viewer's IP address, user agent, and referrer, and can reach hosts routable only from the viewer's network. Chrome and WebKit do not fetch external references on these elements. The impact is a network request to an attacker-chosen URL, not script execution.

Applications that sanitize user-supplied SVG, directly or inside HTML, with Loofah's default allowlist or with `rails-html-sanitizer` with SVG elements permitted are affected.

## Mitigation

Upgrade to Loofah >= 2.25.3.

findings.title: Loofah: CSS url() sanitization bypass via escaped parentheses
findings.summary:
## Summary

`Loofah::HTML5::Scrub.scrub_css` rejected any property whose top-level Crass tokens included a `:url` or `:bad_url`, and left `url` out of the allowed CSS functions. Both checks ran only against the first parse of the `style` attribute. When `scrub_css` rebuilt each property it emitted identifiers with their CSS escapes decoded, so parentheses written as escapes — `url\28 …\29` — hid the `url` token from the checks, and the rebuilt value was re-parsed into a live `url()` that nothing checked again. An escaped property name, six-digit escapes, escaped comments and escaped quotes all reached the same place.

## Impact

A sanitized `style` attribute could make a viewer's browser issue a request to an attacker-chosen URL. `list-style` fetches on render with no interaction, `cursor` on hover. That leaks the viewer's IP address, user agent and access timing, and can reach hosts routable only from the viewer's network. No script survives sanitization and the attacker cannot read the response, so the request itself is the whole impact.

Applications that sanitize user-supplied HTML with Loofah's default allowlist and display it to other people are affected.

## Mitigation

Upgrade to Loofah >= 2.25.3.

## Credit

Reported by NotAFlightRisk through GitHub's private vulnerability reporting.

findings.title: code16/sharp: Arbitrary class instantiation through the embed_key API parameter
findings.summary:
### Impact

An authenticated attacker can instantiate any class in the PHP application by using the `embed_key` parameter across multiple API endpoints. The instantiation is performed by the Laravel container. As a result, the `__construct()` method of the class is called and all constructor dependencies are resolved. The attacker cannot specify parameter values and cannot call any arbitrary method.

### Patches

The problem has been patched in 9.23.0 and pre-release version 10.0.0-beta.4. An additional check was added to verify that `embed_key` is a class extending `SharpFormEditorEmbed` before any instantiation.

### Workarounds

No known workarounds.

findings.title: Bringing Rust to the Pixel Baseband
findings.summary: Posted by Jiacheng Lu, Software Engineer, Google Pixel Team Google is continuously advancing the security of Pixel devices. We have been focusing on hardening the cellular baseband modem against exploitation. Recognizing the risks associated within the complex modem firmware, Pixel 9 shipped with mitigations against a range of memory-safety vulnerabilities. For Pixel 10, Google is advancing its proactive security measures further. Following our previous discussion on "Deploying Rust in Existing Firmware Codebases" , this post shares a concrete application: integrating a memory-safe Rust DNS(Domain Name System) parser into the modem firmware. The new Rust-based DNS parser significantly reduces our security risk by mitigating an entire class of vulnerabilities in a risky area, while also laying the foundation for broader adoption of memory-safe code in other areas. Here we share our experience of working on it, and hope it can inspire the use of more memory safe languages in low-level environments. Why Modem Memory Safety Can’t Wait In recent years, we have seen increasing interest in the cellular modem from attackers and security researchers. For example, Google's Project Zero gained remote code execution on Pixel modems over the Internet. Pixel modem has tens of Megabytes of executable code. Given the complexity and remote attack surface of the modem, other critical memory safety vulnerabilities may remain in the predominantly memory-unsafe firmware code. Why DNS? The DNS protocol is most commonly known in the context of browsers finding websites. With the evolution of cellular technology, modern cellular communications have migrated to digital data networks; consequently, even basic operations such as call forwarding rely on DNS services. DNS is a complex protocol and requires parsing of untrusted data, which can lead to vulnerabilities, particularly when implemented in a memory-unsafe language (example: CVE-2024-27227 ). Implementing the DNS parser in Rust offers
